title: Redundant Nesting — Detection and Elimination
content: Redundant nesting is a wrapper frame that exists only to do something the parent could already do. The most common form: a frame containing a single child, added only to apply padding — that padding should live on the parent instead. How to detect: (1) In the layer panel, look for frames with a single non-component child. (2) Select the frame and ask: does removing this frame change anything except spacing values I could move to the parent? (3) Check Dev Mode — unnecessary wrappers produce nested divs with no functional purpose. How to fix: move the padding/gap from the wrapper to the parent, then delete the wrapper and reparent its child. Benefits: fewer layers, faster navigation, simpler Dev Mode output, better file performance. Exception: a wrapper is justified when it has a background fill, a distinct clip or overflow, acts as a component root frame, or carries an alignment override that truly differs from the parent.

title: Auto Layout Hierarchy Optimization — Flatten Where Possible
content: Every nesting level adds cognitive load and file weight. Optimal AL hierarchy has 3–4 levels maximum for most components: page frame → section frame → component → element. Diagnostic questions for each level: (1) Does this frame have its own background, border, or shadow that separates it visually? (2) Does this frame align its children differently than its parent? (3) Does this frame act as a scroll container or have clip content enabled? (4) Is this a component boundary (root frame of a component or instance)? If all four answers are no, the level is a candidate for flattening. How to flatten: select both the wrapper frame and its parent, use 'Flatten' only for vector work — for AL frames, manually reparent children and delete the wrapper. Rule of thumb: if two adjacent AL frames have the same direction, same sizing mode, and no independent visual treatment, they can almost certainly be merged into one.

title: Single-Child Frame Anti-Pattern
content: A single-child auto layout frame is a red flag. When a frame contains exactly one child and that child is not a component instance or slot, the frame is almost certainly unnecessary. Common causes: (1) Adding a wrapper 'just to add padding' when the padding could go on the parent. (2) Adding a wrapper 'just to add a background' to an element — often the element itself can carry the fill. (3) Copying a frame structure from a different context where the wrapper was needed. Test: select the wrapper, note its padding values, then select its child and check if Cmd/Ctrl+G (group) or direct reparenting achieves the same result. Single-child frames are especially costly inside components — they inflate the layer count of every instance without adding value. The one legitimate single-child pattern: a 'safe area' frame that clips overflow from its one child (e.g., an image container that maintains a fixed aspect ratio with clip content on).

title: Avoiding Same-Direction Nested Auto Layouts
content: Two adjacent auto layout frames running in the same direction (both vertical, or both horizontal) with identical alignment and spacing properties almost always indicate unnecessary nesting. Example: a vertical AL frame inside another vertical AL frame, both set to Fill width, same gap, no visual differentiation — this is one frame's worth of work spread across two. The inner frame adds no structural value. Consolidate: move the inner frame's children directly into the outer frame, inherit the gap setting, and delete the inner frame. When same-direction nesting IS valid: the inner frame has a background fill that creates a visually distinct region (e.g. a highlighted section within a list), the inner frame uses a different gap value from the outer (e.g. tighter spacing for a button group within a card footer), or the inner frame is the root of a component instance.

title: Dev Mode Output — How AL Choices Affect Generated CSS
content: Every AL decision maps directly to CSS. Understanding the output helps avoid structural mistakes that produce bloated or incorrect code. Mapping: Horizontal AL → display:flex; flex-direction:row. Vertical AL → display:flex; flex-direction:column. Wrap AL → display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap. Grid AL → display:grid with grid-template-columns/rows. Hug Contents → width:fit-content or height:fit-content. Fill Container → flex:1 (or flex-grow:1). Fixed → width:Npx; height:Npx. Space Between → justify-content:space-between. Gap → gap:Npx. Absolute position child → position:absolute with top/left/right/bottom. Redundant nesting produces nested divs with only padding — developers often clean these up manually, creating drift between design and code. Build AL structure as you want the HTML/CSS to be structured. Each frame is a div; make sure every div earns its place.

title: Common Auto Layout Mistakes — Diagnosis and Fixes
content: Diagnostic checklist for AL problems: (1) Fixed-width text layer — text clips when content changes. Fix: set text width to Fill Container. (2) Spacer frames between elements — brittle, breaks on resize. Fix: delete spacer, set gap on parent AL frame. (3) Groups inside AL — groups have no defined size and cause unpredictable AL behaviour. Fix: select group, press Cmd/Ctrl+G to convert to frame (or right-click > Frame selection). (4) Both axes Fixed on an inner frame — layout cannot flex. Fix: set at least one axis to Fill or Hug. (5) Inner frame padding duplicating parent padding — adds invisible space. Fix: zero out one set of padding. (6) Icon/avatar set to Fill instead of Fixed — stretches unexpectedly. Fix: set to Fixed at the correct pixel size. (7) Absolute-positioned child in flow — removes child from layout but parent does not account for its space. Fix: decide if the element belongs in the flow or as a true overlay. (8) Hug parent with Fill child — impossible combination. Fix: parent must be Fixed or Fill itself when any child uses Fill on that axis.

title: Slots in Figma — How They Work
content: Slots (Figma 2025+) are designated placeholder areas inside components where instance users can add their own layers without detaching the component. In the component editor, any child frame can be marked as a slot via the right-click menu or the component properties panel. Once marked, the slot frame appears in the instance panel as an editable region. The slot frame itself participates in the component's auto layout tree just like any other child. Key behaviour: content added to a slot by an instance user is scoped to that instance — it does not affect other instances or the master component. Slot constraints define which layer types are accepted (components only, any frame, unrestricted). This replaces the old pattern of detaching instances just to customise content areas.

title: Slots and Auto Layout — Sizing and Interaction
content: Slot frames live inside the component's AL tree and must be sized correctly to behave well when instance users add content. Best practices: (1) Set slot width to Fill Container so the slot expands to the available width. This ensures content added to the slot fills the space rather than sitting at a fixed narrow width. (2) Set slot height to Hug Contents so the slot grows as content is added inside. (3) The parent AL frame containing the slot should also Hug height — this lets the component grow naturally with the slot's content. (4) Avoid Fixed dimensions on slots unless the design requires a strict content area (e.g., a media thumbnail slot that must maintain a 16:9 ratio). Fixed slots require instance users to manage content sizing manually, which creates friction. Pattern: Slot frame → Fill width + Hug height → inside a vertical AL parent that also Hugs height. Result: the entire component grows cleanly as slot content is added.

title: Slots vs Instance Swap Properties — When to Use Each
content: Slots and Instance Swap component properties both allow instance users to customise component content, but they serve different purposes. Instance Swap property: for swapping one component for another at a designated location within a component (e.g., swapping a checkmark icon for an arrow icon). Best for controlled substitution where the replacement is always another defined component. Slot: for adding arbitrary custom content — layers that aren't pre-defined components. Best for open content areas where the user needs to compose freely (e.g., a card body, a modal content area, a toolbar actions zone). Decision rule: if the customisation is 'which component goes here' → use Instance Swap property. If the customisation is 'what content goes here, and I need to compose it myself' → use Slot. You can combine both: a component might have an Instance Swap property for the icon and a Slot for the body content.

title: Building a Component with a Slot — Step-by-Step
content: Recipe for adding a slot to an existing component: (1) Enter component editor (double-click the master component). (2) Add or identify the child frame that will serve as the slot content area. Name it clearly: 'Slot / Content' or '[Slot] Body'. (3) Right-click the frame → Mark as Slot (or use Component Properties panel → + → Slot). (4) Set the slot frame's sizing: Fill Container width, Hug Contents height (for most vertical components). (5) Add slot constraints if needed — restrict to component layers only for controlled design, or leave open for maximum flexibility. (6) Exit the component editor. On any instance, the slot frame now appears as an editable region in the right panel. (7) Test by adding a text layer, an icon, or another component instance directly inside the slot on an instance — verify the parent component resizes correctly. Common gotcha: if the slot frame is Fixed size, content overflows rather than expanding the component. Always verify with Fill + Hug sizing.

meta.shortcut: Right-click child frame → Mark as Slot
